headline: Can’t afford a home? Maybe you should buy one with your parents.
author: Maurie Backman

paragraphs.text: During the third quarter of 2026, the median sales price of a new home in the United States was $393,300. Ten years earlier, it was $303,800. Add in the fact that the average 30-year mortgage rate is above 7 percent, and it’s no wonder so many younger buyers are struggling to purchase a home.

If you’re tired of renting but can’t comfortably afford to buy a home on your own, one solution may be to purchase it with your parents and live there together. There are benefits and drawbacks to this type of arrangement, and it’s important to think through them before moving forward.
The pros
When you team up with your parents to purchase a home, you get more buying power, said Daniel Yoon, a real estate agent with eXp Realty in North Chesterfield, Virginia.

“A parent on the loan can help a young buyer qualify for a higher loan amount,” said Yoon. “In a market with few starter homes, the parents’ assistance can be the difference between renting for two more years and getting the keys.”

Daniel Kramp, a real estate broker at Christie’s International Real Estate New York, said that if parents have enough accumulated wealth to purchase the home without financing it, you can avoid borrowing at today’s higher mortgage rates and save money. Your parents’ contribution may also allow you to purchase a nicer, more spacious place than what you can afford on your own.

Even if you end up with a mortgage payment, splitting it with parents could make it easier to manage, said Yoon. And if you’re close to your parents, being under the same roof could benefit everyone. If you have kids, it may allow your parents to help with child care, and it could make it easier for you to become a caregiver for your parents as they age.
The cons
When you buy a home with your parents, you’re not the only one calling the shots.

“If parents are helping with a big down payment and are co-purchasing with you, they also have a say in where they think you should live,” said Kramp. As a result, you may not end up getting the home you want despite having access to more funds.
Things could also get complicated if circumstances change, Yoon said.
“What if one person wants out in three years and the other wants to stay for 15-plus?” he asked.

Your parents might eventually decide to retire to a warmer place, or you might get a job that requires you to relocate. If one owner leaves, the remaining one could get stuck with a more expensive home than they can afford.

Conflict could also arise over things like maintenance, repairs and improvements. You might prefer to outsource snow removal and lawn mowing. Your parents may not want to pay for services you’re all capable of performing yourselves. These could turn into arguments that sour the arrangement.
Approaching a joint purchase

If you like the idea of buying a home with your parents and living there together, first talk everything through. Discuss what that arrangement could look like and acknowledge some of the drawbacks that might arise, like a lack of privacy or disagreements over upkeep and renovations.

“Parent assistance can get a young buyer into a home where rates and prices of today are out of reach individually. It can also tie a family to an agreement that’s hard to undo,” Yoon said. It’s important to be on the same page, he added, because if a major conflict arises it could affect your relationship, not just your finances.

Next, see if there are properties available in your ideal area that can actually accommodate a multigenerational living arrangement. The conversation may be a moot point if you’re unable to find a home that can meet everyone’s needs.

If you decide to move forward, hire an attorney to write a detailed ownership agreement. Make sure it addresses who’s responsible for the down payment and what percentage each person will contribute; how the mortgage is paid; how maintenance and repairs are handled; and what happens when someone wants out.

It should also specify how the title is held so the home transfers smoothly if a parent passes away. A thorough agreement could protect everyone involved in a joint home purchase and help safeguard family relationships as your finances become more closely intertwined.
